rationale: C04 plausibly supplied a concrete template for substantial portions of the later letter. Both texts defend the steel intervention through the same distinctive sequence: prior voluntary postponement exceeded Taft-Hartley's 80-day delay; invoking that Act would require a board and procedural delay and might not avert a shutdown; uninterrupted steel production is essential to national security; Government operation is distasteful and temporary; and Congress has been invited to prescribe an alternative. C25 contributes related discussion of steel profits and stabilization, while C18 supplies the underlying seizure action and emergency rationale, but neither matches as much of the child's explanatory structure and language as C04.

shared_material.child_excerpt: strike action was delayed, before April 8, for 99 days--voluntarily--whereas the Taft-Hartley Act could have delayed it only 80 days--by compulsion
shared_material.parent_excerpt: We have also had a delay--voluntarily--of 100 days... I see no advantage [in] a compulsory delay of 80 days instead of a voluntary delay of 100 days
shared_material.explanation: Distinctive comparison of the actual voluntary postponement with Taft-Hartley's compulsory 80-day delay.

shared_material.child_excerpt: A Board of Inquiry must be appointed, must hold hearings, and must prepare a report to the President. Only then may the President instruct the Attorney General to seek an injunction. All this takes time.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: The emergency provisions of the Taft-Hartley Act provide for a fact-finding board... The Act provides no means for preventing a shutdown while the fact-finding board is making its inquiry
shared_material.explanation: Both use the Act's procedural machinery and resulting delay to argue that it would not reliably prevent a steel shutdown.

shared_material.child_excerpt: the idea of Government operation of the steel mills is distasteful to me... I have twice sent messages to the Congress asking it to prescribe a course to be followed
shared_material.parent_excerpt: I had ordered temporary operation of the steel mills by the Government with the utmost reluctance; that the idea... was thoroughly distasteful to me... if the Congress wished to take action, I would be glad to cooperate
shared_material.explanation: Close language and the same paired argument: reluctant temporary operation coupled with an invitation for Congress to enact an alternative.

shared_material.child_excerpt: I want to end Government operation at the earliest possible moment... without irreparable harm to the national interest.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: I wanted to see it ended as soon as possible... imperative, for the sake of our national security, to keep the steel mills in operation.
shared_material.explanation: The later letter reuses the temporary-operation framing constrained by national-security necessity.
